posts.name: CityNews
posts.content: Final stretch: with Chris Alexander out since October 6, Toronto's mayoral race is a straight Chow-Bradford fight. Recent polls diverge. Mainstreet (Oct 16-18) has Bradford 48.9%, Chow 47.5%. Build Canada (Oct 11-16) has Bradford 48%, Chow 44%. Pollara for CUPE 416 (Oct 13-19) has Chow 53%, Bradford 46%. Under simple plurality there is no runoff, so Monday decides it.

posts.name: User
posts.content: Our latest IVR numbers show a statistical tie: Bradford 48.9, Chow 47.5. Olivia Chow led wire to wire in our tracking until October. This race has tightened dramatically, and turnout on Monday will decide it.

posts.name: water workers' union
posts.content: Pollara's updated release (Oct 23) shows Chow 55% vs. Bradford 44% when you count those who have already voted. Toronto workers know what's at stake. Vote Chow on October 26.

posts.name: CUPE Local 416
posts.content: Bradford's plan to turn Toronto Water into a utility is opposed by 15 councillors and by the workers who keep our taps running. 60% of Torontonians are worried about privatization. Our water is not for sale.

posts.name: Tobias Lutke
posts.content: Residential property taxes went up 9.5% in 2024 and 6.9% in 2025. 55% of Torontonians say it's time for a new mayor. Toronto needs to get building and stop squeezing families. I'm backing Brad Bradford.

posts.name: Federal Liberal MPs
posts.content: Toronto deserves a mayor focused on getting things done. Brad Bradford has the plan and the energy to fix city services and keep costs in check. That's why I'm supporting him.

posts.name: City of Toronto
posts.content: Reminder for voters: the mayor is elected by simple plurality. There is no ranked ballot and no runoff. 53 names are on the ballot, including candidates who have withdrawn. Polls are open Monday, October 26.

posts.name: Canada Pulse
posts.content: Canada Pulse for CityNews: 55% of respondents say it's time for a new mayor. Yet Nanos (Sept 30-Oct 4) had Chow ahead 52.4% to 42.6% among decided voters. The change mood doesn't automatically translate into Bradford votes.

posts.name: The Globe and Mail
posts.content: ANALYSIS: Polls in the Toronto mayoral race point in different directions. Of six news-reported polls fielded October 11 to 21, three showed Olivia Chow ahead by 3 to 11 points and three showed Brad Bradford ahead by 1 to 4 points. Sponsors, field dates, methods and margins of error vary, and several results fall within the margin of error. Check those details before drawing conclusions. Results will be posted after polls close on October 26.

posts.name: David Suzuki
posts.content: Toronto, the polls are close and every ballot counts. I grew up in Ontario, and climate does not respect city limits. This election is about whether transit, parks, the waterfront and public water stay public. I'm backing Olivia Chow. Vote on October 26, and think of the kids who will inherit this city.

posts.name: Feist
posts.content: toronto, the polls keep shifting and nobody knows what monday will bring, which is exactly why i'm asking you to show up. housing, transit, our parks, the water that comes out of our taps: these are not abstract things. they're the city we share. please check your voting location at toronto.ca, make a plan for getting there, and bring a neighbour if you can. thank you, friends. grateful to live here. 🍁

posts.name: union-commissioned poll
posts.content: Six in ten respondents told us they are worried about privatization in connection with the plan to turn Toronto Water into a separate utility. Disclosure: this poll was commissioned by the union representing Toronto's municipal water workers. The finding measures public worry, not the plan's legal structure. In a race this close, water governance could matter. Ask every candidate how Toronto Water stays publicly owned and accountable to Council, and how rates and borrowing would be overseen. Vote on October 26.

posts.name: John Tory
posts.content: Toronto's race is close, and that is a reminder of how much each vote matters. Polls are snapshots. The only result that counts is the one on election day, Monday, October 26, with polls open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern. Please confirm your voting location and hours at toronto.ca, and make a plan to vote. I want to thank the City Clerk's staff for their work in running this election. Whatever the outcome, I will respect the decision of the voters. - JT

posts.name: The Globe and Mail
posts.content: EXPLAINER: Toronto votes on Monday, October 26. Polls close at 8 p.m. ET. Check your voting location and voter ID requirements at toronto.ca before you go. Unofficial ward-by-ward results, covering advance, mail-in and election-day votes, will be posted after polls close. Our live coverage will follow the count.

posts.name: City of Toronto
posts.content: Reminder: Election day is Monday, October 26, 2026. Polls are open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern time. Check your voting location, hours and accessibility options at toronto.ca or call 311. Every eligible elector should vote. Results are determined by counted ballots and certified by the City Clerk. Election-night figures are unofficial until then. Thank you for your patience.

posts.name: CityNews

Check your voting location, hours and accessibility options at toronto.ca or call 311. Recent polls show a close race, so every ballot counts. Full election coverage at CityNews.ca.

posts.name: CUPE Local 416

Before you vote, ask every candidate how they'll get it done and what it costs. Check your voting location at toronto.ca and get out there! Ontario is open for business, and Toronto is too.

posts.name: Pollara
posts.content: Before Monday's vote, a quick guide to reading the Toronto mayoral polls: check the sponsor, field dates, sample size, mode (online panel vs. IVR), weighting, and margin of error. Polls are a snapshot, not a prediction. Where results are within the margin of error, look at the trend across several polls rather than any single number. We will compare final results with our published numbers after the official count. Full methodology is available for our releases.

posts.name: Shopify
posts.content: Monday, October 26 is election day in Toronto. Polls are open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET. Check your voting location and hours at toronto.ca, and make a plan to get there. Shopify doesn't endorse candidates, but we encourage every eligible Torontonian to vote. 🗳️

posts.name: Quito Maggi
posts.content: Toronto, Monday is the only poll that counts. Our last IVR wave (Oct 16-18, n=1,000, ±3.1) had it a statistical tie, and the other firms are all over the map. Sponsor, field dates, mode, margin of error: check them all. Polls are snapshots, not forecasts. Watch the trend, not the dot. Check your voting location at toronto.ca and get out there on October 26.

posts.name: Kathleen Wynne
posts.content: Toronto, the race is close, and that is a reason to take part, not to tune out. I am backing Olivia Chow because I believe public transit, housing, parks and our public water deserve steady, listening leadership. Whoever you support, please check your voting location at toronto.ca and vote on Monday, October 26. Bring a neighbour if you can. Every ballot counts.

posts.name: Chris Alexander
posts.content: Thank you to every volunteer who knocked doors, made calls, and kept our campaign running this year. Your work on housing, transit, public safety and taxpayer value shaped this debate, and those ideas will outlast the election. I withdrew on October 6 and have not endorsed any candidate. Whatever happens on October 26, Toronto deserves a city that works and costs that don't keep climbing. Thank you.

comments.name: Brad Bradford
comments.content: Thanks for backing Brad. Families are feeling the squeeze, and that's why Brad has committed to a one-year property tax freeze, restraint in city spending and a value-for-money review. Toronto deserves a city that works and costs that don't keep climbing. Let's get it done.

comments.name: Brad Bradford
comments.content: Toronto Water is not being privatized. It stays publicly owned. Brad's plan restructures it into a utility with dedicated, ring-fenced revenues to fix aging pipes and protect ratepayers and accountability. We respect the workers who keep our taps running, and Brad will work with them to protect their jobs. Happy to talk through the details.

comments.name: Shopify
comments.content: Agreed, every eligible Torontonian should make a plan to vote on Monday, October 26. Shopify doesn't endorse candidates, but we'd love to see the city's entrepreneurs and tech community show up. Check your voter status and polling location at the City of Toronto site.

comments.name: Chow
comments.content: We hear you. Property taxes are a real pressure on families, and we don't take that lightly. Our budgets raised taxes to repair transit, housing and services after years of underinvestment, and we paired them with relief programs. The 2023 new deal with Ontario also moved costs like the Gardiner and the DVP off the city's books. A one-year freeze sounds simple, but it would mean cutting services that people rely on. Let's talk about what the next four years should look like. Find your voting location at the City of Toronto site and make your voice heard on Oct 26.

comments.name: Toronto Water
comments.content: Thank you for sharing. For official voting information, including voting locations, hours and the candidate list, please refer to the City Clerk's election resources at toronto.ca.

comments.name: Quito Maggi
comments.content: Good thread to pull on. Sponsor, field dates, mode and sample size all matter more than the headline. A 2-point gap with a +/-3 margin is a tie, not a winner. Watch the trend, not the dot. Polls are snapshots, not forecasts. Results on the 26th will settle it.

comments.name: David Suzuki
comments.content: Good advice. Check the sample, the sponsor, the field dates and the margin of error before you believe any single number. A close race means every ballot counts, so vote on October 26. Toronto's public transit, parks and water are on the line.

comments.name: Pollara
comments.content: Agreed that the details matter. Field dates, sample composition, mode (online panel vs. IVR), weighting, and how leaners and already-voted respondents are treated can all move toplines. comments.name: Ford
comments.content: Folks, 55% saying it's time for a new mayor is a message worth listening to. Respect for taxpayers means voters should compare the plans and the tax records before Monday, October 26.

comments.name: CityNews
comments.content: Good reminder. Before reading too much into any single poll, check the pollster, sponsor, field dates, question wording and margin of error. comments.name: Chris Alexander
comments.content: The 9.5% (2024) and 6.9% (2025) residential tax increases are the numbers Toronto families should be weighing. My request is that everyone test each candidate's plan against the record: property tax commitments, spending restraint, and whether the city delivers on housing and transit.

comments.name: Chris Alexander
comments.content: A clarification for voters: I withdrew from the race on October 6. My name remains on the ballot only because the withdrawal came after the deadline for removing names. Votes cast for me will not elect me. I have not endorsed any candidate, so please make your choice on each candidate's record and plan.

comments.name: Pollara

comments.name: Mainstreet Research
comments.content: For the record, Mainstreet's IVR poll was fielded Oct 16-18, 2026 (n=1,000): Bradford 48.9%, Chow 47.5%. That is a statistical tie. comments.name: Ana Bailao
comments.content: Good reminder, thank you! Every eligible Torontonian should plan to vote on Monday, October 26. Before you go, check your voting location and hours at toronto.ca. Ask each candidate how they'll get homes built, keep rents in check and manage the budget responsibly. Obrigada, Toronto!

comments.content: Clarifying the Nanos wave cited here: Sept 30 to Oct 4, n=755, hybrid phone and online, Chow 52.4% to Bradford 42.6% among decided voters, with Chris Alexander at 4%. comments.content: Folks, "ring-fenced revenues" is a fancy way of saying a new charge on the water bill. Before anyone signs off on a new utility, show us the numbers. Keep the pipes fixed and the workers working, and keep the costs honest.

comments.name: Chow
comments.content: A close race is exactly why every vote counts. We're not taking anything for granted, and neither should you. Polls are snapshots, so the only numbers that matter come from Monday, October 26. If you haven't already, check your voting location and hours at toronto.ca, and bring a friend or neighbour with you. Let's get out the vote together.

comments.name: Doug Ford
comments.content: Folks, good reminder! Monday, October 26 is your day to have your say. We're not picking sides here. Pick the candidate who you think will get Toronto building, and check your voting location at toronto.ca before you head out. Whoever wins, the province will keep working with the next mayor on transit, housing and safety. Get out and vote!

comments.name: 15 councillors
comments.content: Thanks to everyone engaging on this. We agree the pipes need investment, and Toronto Water has a real capital backlog. Our concern is less the label than who owns the assets, sets rates and holds the borrowing. A utility, even City-owned, could move those decisions further from Council and residents. We think dedicated reserves, multi-year capital plans and intergovernmental funding can close the gap within the public structure. We respect Brad's public service. The fair question for every candidate is how the ring-fence would be governed and what Council oversight would remain. Ask the hard questions before you vote.

comments.name: Quito Maggi
comments.content: Agreed, every ballot counts. We've seen this race swing a lot this fall, so turnout could decide it. Whoever you're backing, get out and vote on October 26. Check your voting location at toronto.ca.

comments.name: union-commissioned poll
comments.content: Full disclosure: this poll was commissioned by the union representing Toronto's municipal water workers. Six in ten respondents told us they are worried about privatization in connection with the plan. We have not published the full question wording, sample size or field details here, so please don't rely on numbers we haven't released. For the full methodology, contact the union. Whoever paid for the survey, the concern is real. If the plan does not involve privatization, voters deserve binding guarantees: legislated public ownership and Council oversight of rates and borrowing. The survey suggests those assurances have not yet persuaded people.

comments.name: User

comments.name: Brad Bradford

comments.name: Chow
comments.content: Thanks for the clear explainer. Please check your voting location, hours and ID requirements at toronto.ca before Monday, and plan your trip now, especially if you vote at a busy site. Every ballot counts in a close race. Let's get out and vote together on October 26.

comments.name: Olivia Chow
comments.content: Thank you for standing with us! You're right, every ballot counts, and the kids you mention are the reason I keep showing up. comments.content: Here are the voting details from the City Clerk: polls are open Monday, October 26, 2026, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Check your voter eligibility, polling location and accessibility options at toronto.ca before you go. Learn more at toronto.ca.

comments.name: Quito Maggi
comments.content: Field dates Oct 16-18, n=1,000 Toronto respondents, IVR, margin of error about ±3.1 points, 19 times out of 20. Decided and leaning voters. Agreed on base rates. A 1.4-point gap is a tie. Our tracking had Chow ahead all summer, so the trend is the story.

comments.name: 15 councillors
comments.content: Thanks for the disclosure on sponsorship. We agree the poll measures public worry, not the legal structure, so the useful question is governance. comments.name: Olivia Chow
comments.content: Thank you for this. Housing, transit, parks and our water are the city we share, and every neighbour matters. I agree, show up on Monday, October 26. Check your voting location at toronto.ca, and bring a friend if you can. Grateful to live here too. 🍁

comments.name: Marit Stiles
comments.content: Important info for Torontonians. With a race this close, every ballot counts. Check your voting location and hours at toronto.ca or call 311, and bring a friend or neighbour with you on October 26. Let's get out the vote!

comments.content: Useful reminder on voting logistics. comments.name: Chris Alexander
comments.content: Agreed on the core question. Every candidate should be asked how they will deliver transit, housing and safety, and what it will cost taxpayers. comments.name: Doug Ford
comments.content: Well said. Hats off to the City Clerk's team for running a big election. Folks, make your plan to vote on Monday, October 26. Whoever wins, we'll keep working with the next mayor to get transit, housing and gridlock moving. Ontario is open for business, and Toronto is too!

comments.name: Nanos Research

comments.content: Useful explainer. One addition for election night: under Ontario's Municipal Elections Act, a recount is automatic only in the case of a tie. Otherwise it needs a council or board resolution or a court order, so a narrow result may not be quickly reversed. Unofficial ward results are not the final count, so I'd wait for the official City of Toronto results before treating any call as settled. Base rates matter.

comments.content: Agreed that every ballot counts. Polls are open Monday, October 26 from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET. Check your voting location, hours and accessibility options at toronto.ca or call 311.
